AKBL.summary: Askari Bank scores 80.6/100, driven mainly by fast growth (sales up 26.8% a year and EPS up 17.5% a year over three years), a 7.3% dividend yield paid in each of the last three fiscal years on record, and a share price above its 200-day average. BOP.summary: Bank of Punjab scores 79.5/100, mainly because it looks cheap (P/E 5.5 against a sector median of 6.7), pays a high dividend (10.2% yield, paid in each of the last 3 years on record) and has grown sales and earnings strongly. GHGL.summary: Ghani Glass scores 75.1 out of 100 (HOLD), carried mainly by a cheap valuation (P/E 5.3 against a sector median of 7.4), a 10.1% dividend yield and a share price trending above its 200-day average. Growth is modest: sales rose about 5.9% a year over three years while EPS slipped about 3.7% a year. Only 62% of the data is available, and debt, liquidity and cash flow could not be scored, so the score is only a partial picture.
strengths: Valuation looks low: P/E of 5.3 is about 0.71x the sector median of 7.4.
Dividend yield of 10.1%, with cash payouts in each of the last 2 fiscal years on record and four 10% cash payouts announced in 2026.

Profit recovered in FY2026: net profit Rs 7.23bn (EPS Rs 7.23) versus Rs 5.90bn (EPS Rs 5.90) the year before, and the share price is above its 200-day average and ahead of the KSE-100 by about 9.7 points over a year.
risks: Debt, liquidity, cash flow quality and cash conversion cycle (38% of the scorecard weight) are unscored because balance sheet and cash flow data were not available, so borrowing levels and whether profits turn into cash are unknown.
Profitability is below its starting level: net margin was 14.94% in FY2026 versus 19.89% in FY2023, and EPS is lower than FY2023's Rs 8.10.
A very high yield and low P/E can mean the market expects earnings to fall, or the payout may be hard to sustain; the data cannot confirm either way, and the dividend record covers only 2 years.
checks: In the annual report, check borrowings, finance costs and cash on hand, and whether operating cash flow covers the dividends paid.
Look at why the net margin fell from 19.89% to 14.94% (input costs such as energy and raw materials, pricing, competition) and whether the FY2026 recovery is likely to last.
Read the September 2026 quarterly results and the new CFO's comments, if any, to see whether the earnings trend and dividend payout are holding.

ABOT.summary: Abbott Pakistan scores 75/100 (HOLD), driven mainly by strong profit recovery and a fairly cheap valuation. EPS rose from Rs 30.69 in 2022 to Rs 81.37 in 2025, net margin widened to 10.57%, and the P/E of 10.6 sits below the sector median of 12.3. Only 62% of the data is covered, so debt, liquidity and cash flow, which together carry 38% of the weight, are not reflected in the score.
strengths: Sales grew about 15% a year over 3 years and EPS grew about 38% a year, with net margin up from 6.10% to 10.57%.
Valuation is modest: P/E of 10.6 is about 0.86x the sector median, and the dividend yield is 4.4%.
Cash dividends were paid in both of the last 2 fiscal years on record, and the latest payout (400% of face value) is larger than the previous one (100%).
risks: Debt, liquidity, cash flow quality and cash conversion cycle could not be scored, so balance sheet strength and whether profits turn into cash are unknown.
Earnings are volatile: 2023 profit was only Rs 0.26 billion (0.47% margin) before rebounding, so the recent margin may not be a stable baseline.
The share has lagged the KSE-100 by about 20.8 points over roughly a year, giving a weak price trend score of 36, even though it trades above its 200-day average.
checks: Look at the balance sheet and cash flow statement for borrowings, cash balances and operating cash flow compared with reported profit.
Find out why 2023 profit collapsed and what drove the margin recovery (pricing, costs, currency, one-offs), and whether it is likely to last.
Read the latest quarterly results (period ended September 30, 2026) to see whether growth and margins are holding, and confirm how sustainable the 400% dividend is relative to earnings.

ABL.summary: ABL scores 74.7/100 (HOLD), mainly because it looks cheap and pays a very high dividend. It trades at a P/E of 6.1 against a sector median of 6.7, with a 9.4% dividend yield and cash dividends in every year on record. The growth scores rest on a 3-year trend that hides a weaker latest year: 2025 sales, profit and EPS were all below 2024. The share price is also lagging the market.
strengths: Valuation: P/E of 6.1 is about 9% below the sector median of 6.7
Dividend: 9.4% yield, with cash payouts in each of the last 3 fiscal years and four interim cash dividends of 40% of face value announced in 2026
Growth over 3 years: sales up about 15% a year and EPS up about 18% a year, from a low 2022 base
risks: Latest year was weaker: 2025 profit after tax fell to Rs 35.2bn from Rs 43.1bn (about -18%), EPS to Rs 30.72 from Rs 37.65, and sales fell about 7%. The 3-year growth scores partly mask this
Price trend is poor: below its 200-day average and about 12 points behind the KSE-100 over a year, so the market may be pricing in lower earnings

The scorecard cannot see bank-specific risks: bad loans, capital adequacy, deposit mix, exposure to government securities, interest-rate sensitivity, or cash flow and debt data. A high payout is not guaranteed if earnings keep falling
checks: Confirm why 2025 profit and sales fell, and whether the 2026 quarterly reports show a recovery, using the September 2026 quarterly report
Reconcile the net margin: the stated 11.83% does not match the listed profit and sales (about 26%), so check how the source defines 'sales' and margin for a bank
Check capital adequacy, non-performing loans and whether 2026 earnings cover the Rs 16 per share of dividends declared so far. Also look into the September 2026 unusual-volume notice

AICL.summary: Adamjee Insurance scores 74.7/100 (HOLD), mainly because earnings have grown quickly and the shares look cheap, at a P/E of 5.4 against a sector median of 5.8. The dividend yield of 5.3% and a steady payout record add support, while a weak price trend holds the score back. Revenue growth could not be scored because sales figures are missing, so the picture is incomplete (80.6% data coverage).
strengths: EPS grew about 25.7% a year over 3 years, from Rs 7.39 in 2022 to Rs 14.66 in 2025
Valuation is slightly below the sector median (P/E 5.4 vs 5.8) with a 5.3% dividend yield
Cash dividends paid in each of the last 3 fiscal years on record, with several payouts announced recently
risks: Sales figures are missing, so revenue growth and the true size of the business cannot be judged, and the net margin figures cannot be checked against sales
Net margin has slipped from 15.2% in 2022 to 13.0% in 2025, and from 15.0% in 2024, so profit growth may be slowing in quality

Price is below its 200-day average and trailed the KSE-100 by about 4 points over a year; the scorecard also cannot see debt, cash flow, claims, or investment income, which matter a lot for an insurer
checks: Find premium (revenue) figures and the underwriting result in the annual report to see whether profit comes from insurance business or from investment gains
Read the quarter to 30 September 2026 results (announced Oct 28, 2026) to see whether earnings and margins are holding up
Check the solvency position, claims ratio, and how sustainable the dividend payout is relative to earnings

IMAGE.summary: Image Pakistan scores 74.6/100 (HOLD), driven by strong sales and margin growth and a cheap valuation: P/E of 9.2 against a sector median of 12.3. A weak price trend (below its 200-day average and lagging the KSE-100 by about 14 points) drags the score down. Coverage is only 62%, so debt, liquidity and cash flow are not assessed, and the score is less complete than it looks.
strengths: Sales grew about 21.8% a year over three years, and net margin rose from 10.07% to 14.69%.
Valuation looks modest: P/E of 9.2 is about 0.75x the sector median of 12.3.
Cash dividends were paid in both recorded years, for a yield of about 3.9%.
risks: Debt, liquidity, cash conversion and cash flow quality are unscored because balance sheet and cash flow data are missing, and these carry 38% of the total weight.
EPS growth (7.6% a year) is far slower than profit growth, which hints that the share count increased. Sales growth also slowed sharply in the latest year, to about 2% from 24% the year before.
The price is below its 200-day average and has lagged the KSE-100 by about 14 points over a year, so the market may be seeing something the scorecard cannot.
checks: Check the annual report's balance sheet and cash flow statement for borrowings, interest cost, and whether profits turn into operating cash.
Find out why sales growth slowed in FY2026 and why EPS grew much slower than profit (new shares issued?).
Read the September 2026 quarterly results to see whether margins near 14.7% are holding, and check receivables and inventory levels.

MEBL.summary: Meezan Bank scores 71.8/100 (HOLD), helped by strong three-year growth, a 5.5% dividend yield and a share price trending well above the market. The main drag is valuation: a P/E of 10.3 is about 1.5 times the sector median of 6.7. The growth scores also hide that 2025 revenue, profit and EPS were all lower than in 2024.
strengths: Three-year growth was strong: sales up about 26.5% a year and EPS up about 25.4% a year.
Cash dividends were paid in each of the last 3 fiscal years, with the latest interim payout raised to 80% of face value from 70% a year earlier.
Net margin improved from 19.39% to 21.18% over the period, and the price is above its 200-day average and about 19.5 points ahead of the KSE-100 over roughly a year.
risks: 2025 sales fell about 10% (Rs 285.1bn vs Rs 315.9bn), profit after tax about 12% and EPS from Rs 56.62 to Rs 49.54. The three-year growth figures mask this recent slowdown.
The stock trades at a premium to other banks (P/E 10.3 vs 6.7), which leaves less room for disappointment if earnings keep falling.
The scorecard has no bank-specific data on loan quality, capital adequacy, deposit mix, or debt and cash flow, so balance-sheet strength cannot be judged from it.
checks: Find out why 2025 income and profit declined (for example lower profit rates or higher costs) and whether the September 2026 quarterly report shows a recovery.
Check non-performing loans, provisioning and capital adequacy ratio in the latest annual and quarterly reports.
Confirm that the dividend is covered by earnings, and judge whether the premium P/E is justified by the bank's franchise and growth outlook.

PAKT.summary: PAKT scores 71.7/100 (HOLD), helped mainly by a very high dividend score (yield 8.6%) and steady growth, with sales up 13.6% a year and EPS up 11.9% a year over three years. Valuation is middling: the P/E of 10.8 is exactly the sector median. The score rests on only 62% of the data, because debt, liquidity, cash flow and cash conversion could not be scored, so it says nothing about balance sheet strength.
strengths: Sales rose from Rs 94.9bn (2022) to Rs 139.0bn (2025), and EPS rose from Rs 83.45 to Rs 116.85.
Dividend yield of 8.6%, with cash payouts announced repeatedly in 2026 (most recently 500% of face value on Oct 27).
Net margin is still healthy at 21.5%, and the price is above its 200-day average.
risks: Margins have slipped from 26.3% in 2023 to 21.5% in 2025. EPS has barely moved since 2023 (Rs 113.35 to Rs 116.85), so recent growth is weaker than the 3-year figure suggests.
The 8.6% yield works out to roughly Rs 128 a share at the current price, above 2025 EPS of Rs 116.85. If that is right, the payout may be hard to sustain from earnings alone.
Debt, liquidity, cash flow quality and cash conversion are unscored (about 38% of the weight), so hidden leverage or weak cash generation would not show up here.
checks: Check the cash flow statement and balance sheet: is operating cash flow covering profit and dividends, and how much debt does the company carry?
Compare total dividends per share over the last 12 months with EPS, and read the latest quarter (to 30 Sep 2026) for margin and profit trends.
Find out why margins fell after 2023 (costs, pricing, taxes or volumes) and whether management expects that to continue.

EFERT.summary: Engro Fertilizers scores 71.1 out of 100, which maps to a HOLD signal. Strong sales growth (about 26% a year over three years), steady EPS growth and a 6.8% dividend yield carry the score. Profit margins have slipped, the share trades slightly above its sector's typical P/E, and it has lagged the KSE-100 over the past year. Only 62% of the data is available, so the score says nothing about debt, liquidity or cash flow.
strengths: Sales grew about 25.9% a year over three years, from Rs 96.9bn in 2022 to Rs 193.2bn in 2025.
Dividend yield of 6.8%, with a cash dividend paid in each of the last 3 fiscal years on record and several interim payouts announced in 2026.
EPS grew about 15.5% a year over the period, so earnings have risen along with sales.
risks: Profitability is weakening: net margin fell from 16.18% in 2024 to 12.3% in 2025, and profit after tax and EPS both dropped (EPS Rs 22.62 to Rs 17.80).
Valuation is not cheap: P/E of 11.4 is 1.06x the sector median of 10.8, and the share has underperformed the KSE-100 by about 14.8 points over roughly a year.
The scorecard cannot see debt, liquidity, cash conversion or cash flow quality (about 38% of the weighting), so balance sheet strain or weak cash generation could be hidden.
checks: Find out in the annual and the latest quarterly report why margins and profit fell in 2025 and whether the 2026 nine-month results show recovery or further decline.
Check the balance sheet and cash flow statement for debt levels, interest costs, and whether operating cash flow covers the dividend.
Verify that the dividend is sustainable given lower EPS, by comparing 2026 payouts with earnings per share, and check any gas supply or pricing and policy risks the company discloses.

GADT.summary: GADT scores 70.6 out of 100, and the score leans heavily on valuation: a P/E of 2.7 against a sector median of 6.6. Sales have grown about 9.4% a year, but profit has not kept up. EPS has fallen about 7% a year and net margin is 3.46%, down from 5.68% three years earlier. Only 62% of the data was available, so the score is partial.
strengths: Very cheap on earnings: P/E of 2.7 is about 0.40x the sector median of 6.6
Sales grew from Rs 58.0bn to Rs 76.0bn over the period, and profit recovered from the 2024 low to Rs 2.63bn
Price is above its 200-day average, and a cash dividend was paid (yield 1.7%)
risks: Earnings are volatile: EPS was Rs 117.44 in 2023, Rs 28.35 in 2024 and Rs 93.78 in 2026, so a low P/E may reflect a peak or one-off profit
Debt, liquidity, cash flow quality and cash conversion cycle are not scored (38% of the weight), so balance sheet strength is unknown
The share has lagged the KSE-100 by about 17.9 points over a year, and margins remain below 2023 levels
checks: Check the latest annual report for one-off gains, bonus issues or share splits that could be distorting EPS and the P/E, as the red flag warns
Check borrowings, finance costs, and operating cash flow against reported profit in the balance sheet and cash flow statement
Read the quarterly report to September 30, 2026 to see whether margins are recovering, and compare the 50% cash dividend with earnings

SSOM.summary: S.S.Oil Mills scores 70.2/100 (HOLD), mainly because sales and earnings have grown quickly and the shares look cheaply priced at a P/E of 5.5, in line with its sector median. Weak price momentum and a modest dividend hold the score back. Only 62% of the data is available: debt, liquidity, cash flow and cash conversion could not be scored, so the picture is incomplete.
strengths: Sales grew about 30% a year over three years, from Rs 6.2bn to Rs 13.7bn (figures in Rs thousands in the data).
EPS rose from a loss of Rs 21.74 in 2024 to Rs 70.94 in 2026, and net margin improved to 2.93% from 2.16% at the start of the period.
P/E of 5.5 matches the sector median, and a cash dividend was paid in both years on record.
risks: Earnings are not steady: 2024 was a loss-making year, and margins are thin at under 3.2%, so small cost or price shifts could hurt profit.
Price is below its 200-day average and has lagged the KSE-100 by about 16.5 points over a year, which suggests the market is cautious.
The scorecard cannot see debt, liquidity, cash flow or working capital (about 38% of the weight), so borrowing levels or weak cash generation could be hidden. The dividend yield is also low at 1.1%.
checks: Check the balance sheet in the annual report for total borrowings, interest costs and the current ratio.
Check whether operating cash flow supports the reported profit, and how much cash is tied up in inventory and receivables.
Read the September 2026 quarterly results to see whether the sales growth and the roughly 3% margin are holding, and what caused the 2024 loss.

MCB.summary: MCB scores 69/100 (HOLD), mainly because of a very high dividend yield of 9.2% and strong growth over three years. Valuation holds the score back: the P/E of 8.9 is about 1.3 times the sector median of 6.7. The three-year growth is flattered by a weak 2022 starting point, because sales, profit and EPS have all slipped since 2023.
strengths: Dividend yield of 9.2%, with cash dividends paid in each of the last 3 fiscal years on record and several 90%-of-face-value payouts announced recently
EPS rose from Rs 27.63 in 2022 to Rs 45.73 in 2025, and sales rose from Rs 111.8bn to Rs 181.4bn
Price is above its 200-day average and slightly ahead of the KSE-100 over about a year (+4.7 points)
risks: Earnings have fallen two years in a row: EPS went from Rs 50.32 (2023) to Rs 48.62 (2024) to Rs 45.73 (2025), and profit after tax fell from Rs 59.6bn to Rs 54.2bn. The headline growth rates hide this.
Valuation is a premium to other banks (P/E 8.9 vs a 6.7 sector median), which leaves less room for disappointment
The scorecard cannot see bank-specific risks: bad loans, capital adequacy, deposit mix, interest-rate sensitivity, or exposure to government debt. It also has no cash flow data.
checks: Open the latest quarterly report (period ended 30 Sept 2026) to see whether profit is still falling or has stabilised; the figures here only run to 2025
Check non-performing loans, provisions and capital adequacy in the annual and quarterly reports, since none of these are in the scorecard

Check how the reported net margins (15.7% to 18.4%) are calculated. They do not match profit divided by the sales figures shown, so the revenue definition differs. Also confirm the dividend is comfortably covered by earnings, given the 9.2% yield.
